content.title: WEIRD BODY SIGNALS PEOPLE BLAME ON STRESS (BUT AREN'T)
facts: **White spots on nails** – Often linked to low **zinc**, especially if paired with slow wound healing or a weaker sense of taste.
**Cracked corners of the mouth** – Classic sign of low **iron** or **B2/B12**, not just dry weather like most people assume.
**Restless legs at rest** – Frequently tied to low **iron** stores, even when standard blood tests look 'normal enough'.
**Muscle twitches under the eye** – A common early clue of low **magnesium**, especially during high-stress weeks.
**Bleeding gums when brushing** – Can point to low **vitamin C**, not just 'brushing too hard' like most assume.
**Poor night vision in dim rooms** – One of the earliest signals of low **vitamin A**, long before daytime vision changes.
**Puffy, swollen ankles by evening** – Sometimes linked to low **potassium**, which throws off fluid balance in the body.
**Brittle hair that snaps easily** – Often connected to low **iodine**, which quietly slows down your whole metabolism.
**Tingly, numb feeling in toes** – A frequent early flag for low **vitamin B12**, especially if it's worse at night.
**Bruising from the lightest bump** – Can signal low **vitamin K**, which your body needs to clot and repair blood vessels.

content.caption:
A few of these deserve more than one line. Low **zinc** doesn't just show up as white spots on nails — zinc is involved in making new skin and immune cells, so when levels drop, your body literally can't patch itself up as fast, which is why small cuts or breakouts seem to linger. Restless legs are often brushed off as 'just a weird habit,' but low **iron** affects how oxygen reaches your muscles at rest, and your nervous system reacts with that twitchy, restless sensation when you're lying still. And that puffiness around the ankles by the end of the day? Low **potassium** disrupts the sodium-potassium balance that keeps fluid moving properly through your cells, so it tends to pool exactly where gravity pulls it. Everyone's body is different, so take these as prompts to dig deeper, not a diagnosis.
